opportunities.title: Post-grant survival of academic research web apps
opportunities.narrowed_scope: A-S2a: Static/WASM archival revival of lightweight Digital Humanities and data-explorer research web apps built on officially retired runtimes (e.g., Python 2, PHP 5/7, Flash/Java Applets), targeting university digital scholarship labs and research libraries.
target_users: University digital scholarship labs (e.g., King's Digital Lab, UVic Endings)
Academic research libraries and Research Technical Professionals (RTPs)
opportunities.payer: University libraries, digital scholarship labs, and research infrastructure grants (via project SLAs or institutional budgets; no proven standalone commercial tool buyer)
opportunities.maintainer: Research Technical Professionals (RTPs), university library IT, or OSS academic consortia

cases.case: King's Digital Lab legacy estates & ELIXIR Tools Platform
NBDC Life Science Database Archive (89 archived databases, Japan)

opportunities.consequence_of_inaction: Published scientific tools and interactive research datasets break after 2-5 year grant cycles end, causing citation link rot and loss of non-programmer usability.
opportunities.strongest_alternative: Project Endings static principles + Webrecorder/Browsertrix + NBDC/Zenodo dataset archiving
opportunities.strongest_counterevidence: Wren et al. (2017) suggests highly cited bioinformatics tools mostly survive on their own, while heavy server-side compute apps cannot be staticized without losing core functionality.
opportunities.resurrection_anchor: Officially retired web runtimes (Python 2, PHP 5/7, Flash/Java Applets) only when narrowed to A-S2a; none for generic S2
opportunities.falsifier: Sample 20 open-source DH/bioinformatics web apps past funding and measure what fraction can be converted to static/WASM without losing core query functionality (Task B H8); kill if <30% succeed or deterministic static crawlers match.

demand.basis: Direct institutional activity in NA (UVic), EU (KDL 2026), and Asia (NBDC 89 DBs), though no direct evidence of WTP for a new standalone software tool.

international.basis: Directly verified primary cases in 3 regions (NA, EU, Asia) with named institutional actors and low cross-border legal friction for OSS academic projects.

innovation.basis: Plausible gap between raw data dumps (NBDC/Zenodo) and manual static rebuilds (Project Endings), though Browsertrix/Webrecorder partly covers read-only replay.

theme.basis: Reaches 3 only when narrowed (A-S2a) to apps stranded on officially retired runtimes; generic post-grant maintenance would score 2.

ai.basis: Hypothesized value in migrating undocumented legacy codebases to static/WASM with regression tests, but unproven against conventional refactoring.

feasibility.basis: A scoped prototype converting real open-source legacy research web apps to static/WASM is achievable within 7 days using public academic repos.

demo.basis: Clear before/after demo showing a broken legacy research app running serverless in a browser, though requires brief academic context.

sustainability.basis: Plausible OSS/institutional model backed by university library budgets and grant afterlife clauses, but no verified commercial software buyer.

opportunities.title: Pre-shutdown semantic asset transfer for small platforms
opportunities.narrowed_scope: A-T2a: Pre-shutdown export-to-portable-archive and migration bridge for small community/creator platforms (e.g., Cohost, Glitch, Ameba Ownd) whose native exports drop embedded media, thread structure, or links.
target_users: Departing small-platform operators during sunset windows
Affected creators and niche community admins migrating off dying platforms
opportunities.maintainer: Open-source preservation communities or non-profit archiving organizations (e.g., Internet Archive / Webrecorder ecosystem)

cases.case: EU Data Act cloud switching framework (applicable Sept 2025)
Ameba Ownd service termination & image-URL-only export (Japan, 2026)

opportunities.consequence_of_inaction: Community posts, embedded media, small web projects, and inbound links vanish or degrade into unusable raw dumps once sunset windows close.
opportunities.strongest_alternative: Native platform exports + ArchiveTeam/Wayback Machine + Webrecorder/Browsertrix + competitor importers
opportunities.strongest_counterevidence: Dying operators have zero budget (Cohost ~$17k/mo deficit), living SaaS competitors build their own importers (Glitch), and DTI/DTP does not create WTP for insolvent shutdown tools.
opportunities.resurrection_anchor: Officially discontinued small platforms and web hosts (e.g., Cohost, Glitch, Ameba Ownd)
opportunities.falsifier: Inspect 3-5 real shutdown exports (Cohost, Glitch, Ameba Ownd, one undocumented SaaS) and compare hand-written parsers vs AI schema inference (Task B H2); kill if deterministic parsers match or semantic loss is minor.

demand.basis: Strong 2025-2026 behavioral rescue evidence (Glitch redirects, ArchiveTeam Cohost/Glitch grabs, Ameba Ownd exports), but zero evidence of willingness to pay for a new tool.

international.basis: Direct NA cases (Glitch, Cohost), EU regulatory context (Data Act), and Asian case (Ameba Ownd, snippet-only details); GDPR/privacy rules add cross-border constraints.

innovation.basis: Gaps exist in native exports (e.g., missing media files, flat JSON), but ArchiveTeam, Webrecorder, and competitor importers already cover substantial parts of the job.

theme.basis: Officially shut-down platforms (Cohost, Glitch, Ameba Ownd) anchor a revived portable archive/migration workflow.

ai.basis: Deterministic parsers suffice for structured exports; AI schema mapping for messy exports is unproven and likely replaceable.

feasibility.basis: Feasible within 7 days using legally owned sample exports (e.g., user-owned Glitch/Mastodon/blog export files).

demo.basis: Clear before/after demo turning a dead platform's raw broken export into a searchable, media-intact local archive.

sustainability.basis: No payer found: bankrupt operators have no funds, one-off users resist paying, and third-party scraping carries GDPR/consent friction.

opportunities.title: Preserving disappearing small academic journals
target_users: Editors of small Diamond Open Access journals
Academic libraries and scholarly preservation consortia
opportunities.payer: Academic libraries, national science agencies (JST), and non-profit donors (already funding PKP PN, CLOCKSS, Portico, J-STAGE, SciELO, AJOL)
opportunities.maintainer: Established scholarly preservation consortia (PKP, CLOCKSS, Portico, DOAJ, ISSN)

cases.case: Laakso et al. (174 vanished OA journals) & DOAJ Project JASPER
PKP Preservation Network & Portico (235 trigger events)

opportunities.consequence_of_inaction: Peer-reviewed regional and Diamond OA research disappears permanently from the scholarly record when small publishers lose funding or domain control.
opportunities.strongest_alternative: PKP Preservation Network (free for OJS) + Project JASPER + CLOCKSS + Portico + J-STAGE/SciELO/AJOL
opportunities.strongest_counterevidence: Free and institutional preservation infrastructure already exists (PKP PN, JASPER, Portico); the bottleneck is editorial awareness/enrollment, not missing software, and journals are not a dead technology.
opportunities.falsifier: Audit manifests of small journals transferred via PKP PN or JASPER (Task B H3); already fails Kiroween Resurrection theme gate regardless of manifest completeness.

demand.basis: Strong quantitative evidence (174 vanished OA journals, 235 Portico triggers, 1,318 member libraries), but demand is for enrollment in existing archives, not a new tool.

international.basis: Directly verified primary evidence across NA, EU, Asia (J-STAGE), Latin America (SciELO), and Africa (AJOL).

innovation.basis: Mature free and institutional alternatives (PKP PN, JASPER, CLOCKSS, Portico) already cover the core preservation job.

theme.basis: Fails gate (<3): scholarly journals are not a dead technology, and stretching OJS 2.x EOL (2021) does not address the primary cause of journal disappearance.

ai.basis: OAI-PMH harvesting, BagIt/LOCKSS packaging, and checksum verification are deterministic; AI adds no load-bearing value.

feasibility.basis: Technically buildable, but integrating into trusted scholarly registries (Keepers/CLOCKSS) is an organizational barrier.

demo.basis: Archiving PDFs/XML is visually static and hard to distinguish from existing tools in a 3-minute demo.

sustainability.basis: Institutional budgets already flow to incumbent consortia (Portico, CLOCKSS, PKP); a new entrant lacks a funding path.

opportunities.title: Preserving and transferring digital heritage archives
target_users: Indigenous and community archive stewards (e.g., Mukurtu users, Kulu Language Institute)
University and national heritage archive custodians (e.g., ELAR/BBAW, PARADISEC, Islandora libraries)
opportunities.payer: Philanthropic foundations (e.g., Arcadia Fund), university libraries, and national cultural agencies
opportunities.maintainer: Funded academic stewardship centers (WSU CDSC, BBAW, PARADISEC) and trained community archivists

cases.case: ELAR transfer from SOAS London to BBAW Berlin (2021)

opportunities.consequence_of_inaction: Endangered cultural/language collections risk permanent loss, security compromise on EOL CMS stacks, or loss of Indigenous access-control protocols during custody transfers.
opportunities.strongest_alternative: Mukurtu 4 official migration workflow + Mukurtu Hosting ($350 base) + Islandora + ELAR/PARADISEC
opportunities.strongest_counterevidence: Core bottleneck is community governance, consent, and institutional funding rather than missing software; even the Drupal 7 EOL (Jan 2025) angle is routine CMS replatforming to Mukurtu 4 (Drupal 11), not Resurrection.
opportunities.falsifier: Run a real Mukurtu 3 to Mukurtu 4 migration with custom Cultural Protocols (Task B H4); already fails Kiroween Resurrection theme gate and cannot be ethically demoed with real community data before Dec 4, 2026.

demand.basis: Documented transfers (ELAR SOAS->BBAW) and active Mukurtu 3->4 migration workflows post-Drupal 7 EOL, though bottleneck is governance/staffing.

international.basis: Evidence across NA, EU, Asia (NDL WARP), and Pacific (Kulu/PARADISEC), but strong local legal and Indigenous data sovereignty boundaries apply.

innovation.basis: Mukurtu 4 already provides Cultural Protocols, TK Labels, and official Mukurtu 3 migration docs; gap is mostly staffing and custom-site migration.

theme.basis: Fails gate (<3): heritage custody transfer is not a dead technology; even narrowing to Drupal 7 EOL (Jan 2025) is standard CMS migration (at most 2).

ai.basis: Access-control and Cultural Protocol migration must be 100% deterministic; probabilistic AI risks irreversible cultural/privacy leaks.

feasibility.basis: Validating and publicly demoing real cultural protocol migrations requires community partner consent unattainable within hackathon timeline.

demo.basis: Synthetic heritage data weakens storytelling and requires heavy domain explanation.

sustainability.basis: Relies on philanthropic grants and carries high legal/ethical sovereignty risks if operated by an outside toolmaker.
